item.title: Grand ambitions, petty vision at the Élysée Palace: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 23:24:00
An Aito 9 SUV electric vehicle with programmable LED lighting reading "Paris" on the opening day of the Paris Motor Show in Paris, France, on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. Photo: VCG While the Élysée Palace may "close the door" on Chinese companies at the dinner, it cannot "shut out" Chinese vehicles and technologies from global markets. The "no entry" sign it hangs on Chinese exhibitors epitomizes how France, and Europe at large, are struggling on the industrial track. It is hoped that France can truly play a leading role as a "locomotive" within the EU, rather than saying one thing to China's face and doing another behind its back, which would hardly reflect the statesmanship expected of a major power. France is often portrayed as a nation of romance and warmth. However, the closed-door dinner at the Élysée Palace on the eve of the Paris Motor Show came as a shock. On the evening of October 11, local time, the night before the show's opening, the Élysée Palace held a high-profile dinner reception. While welcoming European exhibitors, it shut the door on Chinese automakers who had traveled far to attend. The Élysée Palace specifically noted that no Chinese exhibitors would be attending the dinner. Such a stark contrast in hospitality sits uneasily with the world's oldest auto show and runs far counter to France's self-proclaimed "great-power aspirations." The dinner was convened for players across Europe's automotive industrial chain to discuss an industrial policy centered on "European preference" and "Made in Europe." Put plainly, it gathered European exhibitors to deliberate on how to tackle the "challenge" posed by China's auto industry. But here is the question: Can Europe's vulnerabilities, exposed amid industrial competition, be fixed over a single dinner? Consumers judge products by their quality, pricing and services, not by who sits beside whom at a banquet table. If the Élysée Palace wants to project a "tough stance" through such a childish "tantrum," it is simply absurd. This gesture inflicts zero harm on Chinese enterprises, yet brings great humiliation to France. This "guest-screening" dinner creates a thought-provoking dissonance with the Paris Motor Show of which it is a part. As a bellwether for the global automotive industry, the Paris Motor Show has always prided itself on openness and competition. In this edition alone, 16 Chinese companies brought more than 20 brands to exhibit. Their representation outnumbers the combined brands from France and Germany, and their exhibition space accounts for one-third of the entire show floor, making China the undisputed major exhibitor. This offers a vivid snapshot of the Chinese auto industry's growth speed, scale and international market appeal. Clearly, while the Élysée Palace may "close the door" on Chinese companies at the dinner, it cannot "shut out" Chinese vehicles and technologies from global markets. The "no entry" sign it hangs on Chinese exhibitors epitomizes how France, and Europe at large, are struggling on the industrial track. The car industry has long been viewed as a pillar of France's national manufacturing. Its relative decline has undoubtedly dented French confidence. To ease its strategic anxiety, France has, to some extent, emerged as the standard-bearer of European trade protectionism against China. The European Commission's decision two years ago to impose anti-subsidy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) was pushed forward with French involvement. France has revised its car purchase subsidy rules, introduced carbon footprint accounting, and leveraged the EU's proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. It seeks to restrict Chinese firms' investment and access to public procurement in Europe, tighten its foreign investment screening regime, and raise compliance costs for Chinese products through EU green trade barriers. These moves lay bare France's strategic anxiety and expose a growing cognitive dissonance within Europe. However, decoupling from the Chinese economy is neither realistic nor logical. China has become a major global manufacturing hub and innovation center for batteries, EVs, charging infrastructure and intelligent vehicles, with deeply intertwined interests with renowned European automakers and suppliers such as Volkswagen, BMW and Bosch. Europe has more than a century of automotive history and is home to numerous iconic global brands. Its commitment to manufacturing excellence and product quality offers valuable lessons for Chinese companies. Likewise, Chinese firms' experience in rapid advances in new energy vehicles, battery components and the application of intelligent technologies offers valuable experience for European industry peers to draw upon. At the government level, China has always welcomed foreign enterprises to invest and thrive in its market. Tesla's factory in Shanghai and Volkswagen Group's increased investment in the Chinese market demonstrate an approach that promotes cooperation through openness and drives innovation through competition. This is perhaps something Europe would do well to learn from. In fact, there is only one fundamental question that France, and Europe as a whole, needs to answer: Does it want an automotive industry that embraces open competition and succeeds on its own merits, or one that survives in a protected greenhouse, sheltered by government policies and insulated from outside competition? Faced with increasingly fierce international competition, it is understandable that Europe's automotive industry is under pressure and that European companies are seeking to join forces. But if the purpose of such actions is not to pool resources for technological breakthroughs and develop new vehicles that can compete in the market, but instead to erect trade barriers against China, the outcome is hardly difficult to predict. History has the answer. Europe has already fallen far behind China and the US in the digital economy. Unless it addresses this weakness in high technology, Europe's manufacturing sector, including its automotive industry, will inevitably face accelerating decline. What Europe needs is open and candid dialogue with China. Not long ago, the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism concluded, with the two sides reaching consensus on a list of 16 outcomes. Further communication is needed to explore concrete ways to properly manage differences within the framework of World Trade Organization rules. These positive political signals will contribute to the healthy development of China-EU economic and trade relations. It is hoped that France can truly play a leading role as a "locomotive" within the EU, rather than saying one thing to China's face and doing another behind its back, which would hardly reflect the statesmanship expected of a major power.

item.title: GT Voice: Here is why China's debt level won't limit macro policy space
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 23:02:00
A view of the Lujiazui area in Shanghai Photo: VCG Some Western media outlets have recently revived their pessimistic take on the Chinese economy, with some hyping the claim that a "growing debt burden limits space for economic stimulus." Such claims have been proven wrong before and lack any solid foundation this time around, as China's debt level remains lower than that of many major economies, the country has taken concrete steps to address the debt issue, and it retains ample policy room to ensure stable, high-quality growth. China's government debt ratio is much lower than the average levels of both major developed economies and major emerging markets. As of the end of 2025, China's total government debt stood at 102.5 trillion yuan ($15.32 trillion), including 41.2 trillion yuan in central government debt, 54.8 trillion yuan in statutory local government debt and 6.5 trillion yuan in hidden local government debt, according to a State Council report published in August. Is that debt level high? Under the broader measure used by the IMF, which includes more local government financing vehicle debt in the government sector, China's total government debt is expected to be around 107 percent of GDP around 2026. By comparison, the US is projected at about 126 percent during the same period, and Japan at more than 200 percent, according to some estimates. In other words, China's government debt is not the highest among major economies. Now, would such a debt level limit China's space for economic stimulus as suggested? To answer that, one must first understand that China has not taken the old road of excessive reliance on aggressive policy stimulus. In recent years, its ongoing efforts to resolve local government debt, advance debt swaps, and optimize the structures of debt maturity have made marked progress. While these moves may impose short-term constraints on the scale of fiscal expansion, they are systematically defusing risks - thereby laying a far more solid foundation for steady, sustainable growth over the long run. As for the inflation landscape, China's consumer price index rose 0.4 percent month-on-month in August, reversing a 0.1 percent decline in July, while year-on-year growth picked up to 0.8 percent. The producer price index rose 0.4 percent month-on-month, reversing a 0.7 percent drop the previous month, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. Both gauges indicated overall moderate price increases. Meanwhile, the IMF in July raised its 2026 headline inflation forecast by 0.3 percentage points to 4.7 percent, compared with its April outlook. Despite global inflationary pressure, China's prices have remained stable. China neither faces the high-inflation constraints that once plagued Europe and the US, nor the policy dilemmas currently confronting many major economies. Crucially, there is still ample room for China's monetary and fiscal policies. China's central bank has made clear that the average reserve requirement ratio (RRR) for financial institutions stands at 6.3 percent, leaving room for further cuts. Monetary policy can act flexibly based on actual economic conditions, releasing liquidity through RRR cuts, policy rate reductions, and targeted structural tools. The ultimate litmus test of an economy's policy space is whether its growth targets can be met. In the first half of this year, China's GDP reached 69.6 trillion yuan, growing 4.7 percent year-on-year, a pace in line with the full-year growth target. Compared with the first half of last year, GDP increased by 3.6 trillion yuan - the largest increment for the period in the past five years, which speaks for itself as the most compelling proof of resilience. In its July outlook, the IMF downgraded this year's global growth forecast to 3 percent while raising China's full-year growth forecast to 4.6 percent. This in itself shows that the international community's assessment of China's economic performance does not align with the pessimistic narrative in certain Western media. The consumer market continues to expand, new growth points such as services consumption and experiential consumption are being cultivated, household income is rising steadily, and the foundation of domestic demand is being consolidated. Boosting domestic demand does not depend solely on large-scale fiscal spending. Structural reforms, including improving the business environment and revitalizing the private sector, all serve as drivers of demand. Fiscal spending is only one tool in the policy toolkit. Tying the recovery of domestic demand exclusively to massive stimulus reflects outdated thinking. China maintains a well-stocked macro policy toolkit with ample room for counter-cyclical regulation. Together with the endogenous momentum unlocked through structural adjustment and reform, these elements form the overall resilience of the Chinese economy. Global Times

item.title: China sanctions Paraguayan, Belizean ministers over Taiwan question, delivering explicit warning of 'no bargaining over one-China principle'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 22:13:00
China's Foreign Ministry The Chinese Foreign Ministry on Monday announced a series of countermeasures against Paraguayan and Belizean ministers over Taiwan-related issues. In both releases, the ministry said that "certain anti-China politicians" in Paraguay and Belize, out of self-serving interests, stubbornly backed their countries' maintenance of the so-called "diplomatic ties" with China's Taiwan region, while making a string of "egregious remarks and actions" on China-related issues, harming China's core interests. Gustavo Emigdio Villate Samaniego, Paraguay's minister of information and communication technologies, and Francis Fonseca, Belize's minister for foreign affairs, foreign trade, education, culture, science and technology, are denied visas or entry into China, including its Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions, according to the ministry. All organizations and individuals within China shall be prohibited from engaging in transaction, cooperation and other activities with them, the ministry added. Both countermeasures rest on the same legal basis, citing Articles 3, 4, 6, 9 and 15 of the Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law of the People's Republic of China. The decision shall take effect on Monday. Pawn of secessionists In response to questions related to the sanctions, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a press conference on Monday that certain politicians from Paraguay and Belize have acted as "chess pieces" for the DPP authorities in their pursuit of independence by soliciting external support. Their visits to Taiwan island and reception of "Taiwan independence" separatist forces in their countries constitute severe interference in China's internal affairs. They also attacked and smeared China by spreading the "Chinese cyber attack" disinformation, causing egregious impact in the world, the spokesperson said. For diehard supporters of "Taiwan independence" separatist forces, China will take all necessary punitive measures to firmly safeguard national sovereignty and territorial integrity, Mao said. The Global Times found that the two sanctioned officials from Belize and Paraguay both maintain close collusion with the DPP authorities. Two days before China announced the sanctions, Villate of Paraguay posted on the X platform to congratulate the Taiwan region on its self-claimed "national day." Citing Paraguayan media ABC Color, Taiwan-based media udn.com reported that Villate was included on the guest list for DPP leader Lai Ching-te's inauguration in May 2024. According to udn.com, Belize's Fonseca also took part in Lai's inauguration in 2024. Before that, he visited the island in March of 2022. In September this year in Belize, Fonseca met with Lin Chia-lung, head of "external affairs" authority of Taiwan island. During the meeting, Fonseca reaffirmed support for the island's so-called "international participation" and voiced optimism over prospects for expanded "bilateral trade," per the udn.com. Taiwan-based media noted that the latest sanctions marked the first time the Chinese mainland has imposed sanctions against officials from the island's so-called "diplomatic allies." Xin Qiang, director of the Taiwan Studies Center at Fudan University, told the Global Times on Monday that previously China's sanctions mainly targeted politicians from Western countries who back secessionists. Extending sanctions to officials from Taiwan's so-called "diplomatic allies" sends a clear and strong signal. With DPP authorities seeking the so-called international space, internationalizing the Taiwan question, and the rising provocation to the one-China principle especially from the island's "allies," China's countermeasures are necessary, said Xin, adding that China's policy and legal toolkit is growing, offering more tools to penalize foreign politicians provoking trouble over the Taiwan question. "This round of sanctions once again demonstrates that the one-China principle brooks no violation. The Chinese government will not turn a blind eye and will mete out punishment to any country or individual that violates this principle," Zhang Wensheng, deputy dean and a professor at the Taiwan Research Institute at Xiamen University, told the Global Times on Monday. Explicit warning Besides their multiple visits to Taiwan island, the two sanctioned officials boast backgrounds in technology and trade. Citing Paraguay's La Nación, the udn.com reported that Villate has over 20 years of experience in the private tech sector and is a founding partner of tech firm E-Services. In June this year, according to the udn.com, Villate discussed cooperation plans on AI computing power centers with visiting officials from the Taiwan region. As early as March 2024, he made a visit to Taiwan island to inspect its semiconductor industry. According to Taiwan-based media Tai Sound, Belize's Fonseca also inked a "memorandum of understanding" with visiting DPP authorities' officials in late September. Zhang noted that the two sanctioned officials' economic and tech backgrounds show the two nations hope to reap dividends from the semiconductor sector, while the Taiwan authorities seek to lure them with its semiconductor strengths. Echoing Zhang, Xin said that as the traditional tactics have borne limited fruit, the DPP authorities have thus stepped up collusion with external forces in tech and trade, leveraging its relative edge in chips. Those most provocative officials have naturally become key targets of China's countermeasures. In addition, observers said the sanctions carry representative significance. Both targeted officials are from Latin American and Caribbean nations, and seven of Taiwan authorities' 12 so-called "diplomatic allies" belong to this region "Such targeted sanctions also serve as an explicit warning to politicians in other Latin American and Caribbean nations who collude with the DPP authorities and attempt to reap gains across the Taiwan Straits that there is no room for bargaining on the one-China principle," said Zhang. Xin said Latin America and the Caribbean once formed a core stronghold for the Taiwan authorities to maintain their so-called "diplomatic relations." In recent years, multiple countries including Honduras, Nicaragua and Panama have severed ties with the Taiwan authorities and established diplomatic relations with the Chinese central government, causing the collapse of the foothold. "This shows that abiding by the one-China principle better serves their long-term development interests," said Xin. "China will take countermeasures against any provocation from the few remaining nations [that have ties with Taiwan authorities], yet it welcomes them if they can get back on the right track." "We also advise the few remaining so-called 'diplomatic allies' of the Taiwan authorities not to be repeatedly manipulated and exploited by secessionists. Tying themselves to such separatist forces leads to no future. They will only miss development opportunities and become isolated from the international community," Mao Ning said on Monday.

item.title: China, EU unveil fresh outcomes in auto trade talks; strong Chinese presence at Paris Motor Show 'underscores potential for deeper co-op'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 22:06:00
An Aito 9 SUV electric vehicle with programmable LED lighting reading "Paris" on the opening day of the Paris Motor Show in Paris, France, on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. Photo: VCG China and the EU have made fresh progress in automotive trade, following recent in-depth discussions on hybrid and electric vehicle (EV) trade under their trade and investment consultation mechanism. A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said on Monday that the two sides have maintained dialogue under the mechanism and reached a series of consensuses and outcomes, which will help maintain a stable and balanced trade partnership between the two major economies. Against the backdrop of rising global trade protectionism and the accelerating transformation of the global automotive industry, it is of particular significance that China and the EU have achieved practical results through consultations on an equal footing, a Chinese expert said, noting that this joint effort demonstrates that both sides have the willingness and capability to properly resolve trade disputes through dialogue. Meanwhile, with around 20 Chinese automotive brands participating in the Paris Motor Show, which opened on Monday, the potential for further China-EU cooperation in the automotive sector, including markets, technology and investment, has become increasingly evident. Important consensus China and the EU have held intensive consultations on hybrid and EV trade based on the principles of mutual respect and equal consultation, seeking to address trade and economic differences while accommodating each other's concerns, a MOFCOM spokesperson said on Monday. The remarks were made in response to a media inquiry about the recent in-depth China-EU discussions on hybrid and EV trade under their trade and investment consultation mechanism, which helped prevent tensions from escalating, as well as speculation by some foreign media outlets over the volume and other details of the hybrid vehicle trade arrangements. The MOFCOM spokesperson said that the two sides emphasized and confirmed three basic principles on hybrid vehicles. According to Eurostat data, EU imports of hybrid vehicles from China stood at 107,000 units in 2024 and 302,000 units in 2025. Building upon the 2025 figures, the two sides reached an arrangement for upward adjustment to ensure export capacity and stable growth for Chinese enterprises, while addressing the realistic and legitimate concerns of industries on both sides. The two sides also agreed that no measures will specifically target Chinese products, let alone subject Chinese enterprises to discriminatory treatment. The quotas allocated to China will be no less favorable than those granted to any other source of imports for the EU, according to the MOFCOM spokesperson, adding that both sides affirmed that trade arrangements should comply with WTO rules and that the Chinese side reserves all rights, including recourse to dispute settlement and demands for trade compensation, within the WTO framework. On the subject of EVs, the spokesperson noted that the two sides secured a "soft landing" for the EU's countervailing duty case in January this year, when the EU issued general guidance on price undertakings, and that the EU will continue to advance procedures for company-specific price undertakings and other review processes under the EV case. Based on equality and mutual benefit, the aforementioned consensus effectively safeguards the interests of Chinese enterprises and averts an escalation of trade friction between China and the EU; it also provides a stable, predictable, and sustainable environment for trade and investment, thereby fostering the stable, balanced, and healthy development of bilateral economic and trade relations, the spokesperson said. The two sides approached the consultations with "limited time and limited objectives," while taking full account of each other's concerns. Reaching a series of concrete outcomes under such circumstances was no easy task, Jian Junbo, director of the Center for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University's Institute of International Studies, told the Global Times on Monday. This once again demonstrates that China and the EU have both the willingness and capability to properly manage their differences and deepen cooperation through dialogue and consultation, Jian said. Against the backdrop of a complex and volatile global trade environment, preventing trade tensions from escalating further will help safeguard business interests and stabilize market expectations, while also providing a useful example for addressing other trade and economic issues between the two sides, said the expert. Window of opportunity Stella Li, Executive Vice President of BYD and CEO of BYD Americas, speaks during the presentation of the Denza Z electric sport car, a sub-brand of BYD group, at the 91st edition of the international Paris Motor Show at the Porte de Versailles in Paris on October 12, 2026. Photo: VCG The progress in China-EU automotive trade talks comes as Chinese automakers step up their presence in Europe, highlighting the importance of a stable and predictable trade environment for deeper industrial cooperation. More than 60 automakers are expected to participate in this year's Paris Motor Show, with Chinese brands particularly prominent, French automotive news website Automobile Actu reported. The number of participating Chinese automakers has doubled compared with the previous edition, with BYD, Leapmotor, XPeng, Geely, Chery, Changan and GAC among the exhibitors, accounting for roughly one-third of all participating automakers. These Chinese automakers are showcasing their latest products and technologies, ranging from pure electric and hybrid vehicles to smart cockpits and fast-charging solutions. On Monday, Chinese auto brand AITO showcased several of its flagship models and latest technological innovations at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, the Global Times learned from the company. The Chinese auto company also unveiled its European market entry and development plans, announcing that it will enter the European market in autumn 2027, marking a significant step in its global expansion. Clifford Kang, a member of the Board of Directors and Vice President of Seres Group, said at the auto show that from technological innovation to international expansion, AITO is moving toward a broader global market. Entering Europe marks an important step in AITO's commitment to sharing a new vision of luxury with its customers. A representative from XPeng told the Global Times that the company will showcase a range of new-energy vehicles, along with its flying car and humanoid robots, at the Paris Motor Show. In terms of research and development, XPeng has established eight R&D centers worldwide, including its European R&D center in Munich, Germany. On the manufacturing front, the company has launched three localized production projects overseas, including one in Austria. Chinese automakers have vast market opportunities in Europe. "There is no need for Europe to view the entry of Chinese automakers simply as a threat to its domestic industry... Instead, the two sides can achieve mutual benefits through technological cooperation, joint research and development, and collaboration across industrial and supply chains," Zhang Xiang, a visiting professor in the engineering department of Huanghe Science and Technology University, told the Global Times on Monday. There are already numerous examples of cooperation between Chinese and European automakers. European automotive giant Stellantis and China's Leapmotor have established a joint venture to expand into international markets, while Germany's Volkswagen Group and China's XPeng have joined forces in EV development and technological research. Zhang said that these partnerships demonstrate that beyond competition, the Chinese and European automotive industries are highly complementary, with considerable potential for mutually beneficial cooperation. From the positive consensus reached in China-EU automotive trade consultations to the strong presence of Chinese automakers at the Paris Motor Show, these developments demonstrate that despite competition and differences in the automotive sector, considerable room remains for the two sides to deepen cooperation, Chinese experts said. "For China and the EU, properly resolving trade disputes through dialogue and providing businesses with a fair, stable and predictable business environment will not only support the long-term development of their respective automotive industries, but also serve their shared interests in advancing the global automotive industry's green transition," said Jian.

item.title: Chinese pilots reveal more on China-Egypt drills: J-16, KJ-500 offsetting disadvantage of being outnumbered by Rafale, MiG-29
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 22:05:00
A Chinese J-16 fighter Photo: VCG Chinese state media aired a news program on Sunday featuring Chinese pilots who took part in the China-Egypt "Eagles of Civilization 2026" joint air training exercise from mid-August to early September, revealing fresh details from the drills featuring J-16 and Rafale fighter jets, including air combat tactics, refueling operations and candid exchanges between the two sides. An expert provided deeper insight into what the new details reveal. The exercise was not only an exchange of air force tactics between the two countries, but also an in-depth showcase of air force equipment development, reshaping perceptions of China's defense strength and defense industry in the Middle East, CCTV News reported on Sunday. An earlier report noted that on the first flight training day, Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) J-16s conducted air combat drills against Egyptian MiG-29 and Rafale fighters. A Chinese expert said this was the first joint exercise featuring both the J-16 and the Rafale, reflecting strong mutual trust and a high level of coordination between the two air forces. In the new CCTV footage, Wei Yuexin, a PLA Air Force pilot who served as tower command on the first day of training, said Egyptian fighters had displayed stronger close-combat maneuverability than their Chinese counterparts that day. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Monday that both the Rafale and MiG-29 are medium-weight fighters with relatively good agility, while the J-16 is a heavy fighter optimized for air-to-ground and air-to-sea strikes while retaining air combat capability. The Egyptian jets' advantage lies in close-range "dogfighting," roughly on par with China's J-10C. However, when it comes to beyond-visual-range combat, the J-16 should perform well, especially when guided by the KJ-500 early warning aircraft, Song said. This was one of the key lessons drawn from the training with the Egyptian Air Force, identifying each other's weaknesses, strengths and gaps, Song said. That lesson showed up later in the drills. CCTV reported that on the third day of training, the joint exercise escalated from single-aircraft and two-on-two engagements to a four-versus-six beyond-visual-range air combat scenario. China deployed four J-16s, while Egypt sent two Rafales and four MiG-29s. Facing this numerical disadvantage, China sent up a KJ-500 early warning aircraft for system-based operations. The KJ-500 can operate in complex electromagnetic environments, conducting surveillance, tracking and identification of conventional targets, and serves as a key airborne command hub. "When the air battle started, we forgot about the numerical disadvantage and forgot that they might be Rafales. We only remembered the timeline for missile evasion. We just needed to evade their weapons, and through tactical coordination, we made up for the numerical gap," Wei was quoted by CCTV as saying. He recalled that after that day's training, at 9:30 pm, Egyptian pilots were still looking for them, hoping to discuss the day's air combat. "What impressed me most was how much they appreciated and were interested in our use of electronic jamming. They thought our timing and jamming capability were excellent," Wei noted. Song commented that future air combat and system-based operations are not just about numbers, but about quality and systems. So while China may have only had four J-16s, it held a qualitative advantage. The KJ-500 acts as a "force multiplier," allowing the J-16, with its large weapons payload and long-range air-to-air missiles, to maximize its strengths and offsetting the numerical gap. The new CCTV video also showed more footage of a PLA Air Force YU-20A tanker refueling Egyptian Rafale fighters multiple times. On August 31, an official spokesperson for the Egyptian Armed Forces posted a photo on X showing the midair refueling, drawing widespread attention. A PLA YU-20A tanker refuels an Egyptian Rafale fighter. Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News "Egypt only has buddy refueling between MiG-29s, so they really valued this joint training opportunity," Wei was quoted by CCTV News as saying. The YU-20A's multiple refueling of Rafales and MiG-29s was extremely valuable experience for the Egyptian Air Force, Song said. As Wei noted, Egypt conduct buddy refueling between MiG-29s, which carries limited fuel and can leave the other MiG-29 with limited combat capability. The YU-20A, by contrast, can refuel any compatible fighters, with the core goal of giving other fighters greater range and endurance, which is critical. The performance of Egyptian Air Force pilots won praise from their Chinese counterparts. Wei said that while their refueling success rate and maneuvers may not have matched China's, "they improved very quickly, and by the end, their success rate had risen very fast." Egyptian pilots, in turn, spoke highly of their Chinese counterparts. One Chinese pilot said in the CCTV report, "When we chatted, they praised not only our skills but also our J-16 fighters and PL-15 missiles. I could feel it in their eyes. They were giving a thumbs-up to our country's development." The Chinese and Egyptian air forces held the Eagles of Civilization 2026 joint training exercise in Egypt from mid-August to early September. The training focused on subjects such as air combat tactics, air superiority operations and combat search and rescue, and included force employment drills, China's Defense Ministry spokesperson Senior Colonel Chen Xi said on August 14. As the second iteration of its kind, the exercise further enhanced mutual trust and traditional friendship, deepened substantive cooperation between the Chinese and Egyptian militaries, and contributed to regional peace and stability, Chen said.

item.title: China's Nebula-2 reusable rocket featuring 'chopstick-style' recovery system advances as key 5-meter-diameter propellant tank rolls off production line
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 22:04:00
Nebula-2 reusable rocket Photo: CGI provided by the Deep Blue Aerospace The 5-meter-diameter stainless steel propellant tank, a key component of China’s commercial reusable launch vehicle Nebula-2, has recently rolled off the production line, marking a major step forward in the rocket’s intensive engineering development phase, the Global Times learned from its developer, Wuxi-based commercial space startup Deep Blue Aerospace, on Monday. The rocket is designed to feature a “chopstick-style” in-situ capture system, which could eventually allow it to be caught at the launch site rather than landing at a separate location. Propellant tanks are structural backbones of rockets and one of the key components affecting the pace of large-scale rocket production and delivery. From design to manufacturing of the 5-meter-diameter stainless steel propellant tank, it set a new record for large-diameter stainless steel rocket tank production in China’s commercial space sector, and paving the way for a second-stage propulsion system test for the Nebula-2 rocket planned for year-end, the Science and Technology Daily reported on Monday. The Nebula-2 rocket can carry up to 25 tons to low Earth orbit. Its first stage is equipped with 11 Thunder-RS engines delivering 12,446 kilonewtons of liftoff thrust, while its second stage uses a single vacuum-optimized engine. The Nebula-2 is designed for more than 20 reuses and features a “chopstick-style” in-situ capture system which could eventually enable the rocket to be captured at its launch site rather than landing at a separate location, improving launch, recovery and reuse efficiency. At present, the development of Nebula-2 is progressing smoothly, with its structural, propulsion, recovery and navigation, and ground tracking, telemetry and control systems advancing steadily on schedule. With its high payload capacity and cost-effectiveness, Nebula-2 is designed to support a wide range of missions, from large-scale satellite constellation deployment for China’s satellite internet network to launching high-value medium- and large-sized satellites into geosynchronous transfer orbit (GTO), medium Earth orbit (MEO) and other orbits for domestic and international customers. China is pursuing multiple technological approaches to reusable rocket recovery, with progress in 2026 highlighting the country's efforts to develop more flexible and cost-effective launch capabilities. On July 10, the Long March-10B successfully completed a sea-based recovery of its first stage using a net system mounted on an offshore platform, marking China's first successful recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster. On August 19, the Zhuque-3 Y2 rocket developed by private aerospace firm LandSpace achieved the country's first successful land-based recovery of an orbital-class rocket's first stage using deployable landing legs.

item.title: US secures diesel while Europe continues to pay the price of Russian sanctions
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 21:49:00
Photo: IC For years, the US has been leading the push to sanction Russia and cut off the revenue Moscow needs to fund the war in Ukraine. Europe took that mission seriously. Now, just as Washington needs more diesel, it is turning back to Russian supplies. The Spectator, a British news magazine, called the deal a "betrayal." The Guardian warned of a fresh crisis with NATO allies, while CNN said it drove a wedge through the Western alliance. It began earlier this month when the US announced a diesel supply arrangement with Russia, alongside a temporary easing of related sanctions. Under the announced plan, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately thereafter. Washington made the rules. Now, Washington is making the exceptions. Why? Observers said that with midterm elections approaching, lower fuel prices are politically attractive. Diesel powers farm machinery, trucks, construction, mining and much of heavy industry. When prices rise, costs ripple through supply chains and end up in household bills. When sanctions collide with domestic economic pressures, Washington is willing to reconsider the rules. Morality remains the slogan. Allies continue to bear the costs. National interests call the shots. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas rejected suspending sanctions on Russian diesel. Germany and the UK said they would maintain sanctions. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal called the US decision a "major miscalculation." Since 2022, Europe has worked hard to reduce its dependence on Russian energy, accepting higher costs in pursuit of broader security goals. The shift was never cost-free. Before the war, Russian supplies of natural gas, oil, and refined products were central to Europe's energy mix. Cheap, reliable energy provided European industry with a competitive edge and underpinned years of economic growth. Yet nowadays, these energy ties have been deliberately severed. Europe had to restructure its sourcing, infrastructure, and logistics. Businesses have faced rising costs and greater uncertainty, factories have moved abroad, prices have remained elevated, and the European economy has continued to suffer. Now the US is making an exception for itself while Europe is still paying. Yet some European politicians would rather keep importing at high prices and continue repeating slogans than admit that almost completely cutting off cheap Russian energy was a self-harming decision. The US is flexible for its own interests, while some European leaders remain ideologically committed to confrontation, refusing to consider even a pause in energy hostilities or the possibility of cooperation. This is not principle; it is a trap of their own making. If Europe stays locked in that position, ordinary Europeans will continue to pay much of the bill. Europe's anger exposes a contradiction that has long existed but is often covered by grand slogans. The US and Europe share many interests, but that does not mean their interests will align forever. An alliance may simply mean standing together when conditions are favorable. When the wind turns, the strongest partner often has the greatest freedom to change direction, leaving others stranded. Europe now faces a choice without easy answers. If it sticks with sanctions, it must continue to bear the costs and explain to the public why those costs are still worth paying. If it relaxes sanctions, it must confront whether its earlier policy goals were wrong. Both paths carry costs. Neither will allow Europe to escape the energy crisis overnight. But the episode offers a lesson to Europe: Energy security should be about keeping Europe running, not sticking to a political line at any cost, and it cannot depend on the assumption that another country will always act in your interests. Resilience in supply chains, strategic reserves, and diversification of sources are not optional choices; they are questions of survival. Never hand the lifeline of your energy supply to someone else - even if they call you an "ally."

item.title: NHK documentary on notorious Yasukuni Shrine sparks backlash, exposing deep-rooted misconceptions among right-wing forces: Chinese expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 21:17:00
Japanese citizens hold a protest march near Awaji Park in Tokyo on August 15, 2026, opposing politicians offering ritual fees to or visiting the notorious Yasukuni Shrine, which enshrines Class-A war criminals from World War II. Photo: VCG A new documentary on Japan's notorious Yasukuni Shrine aired by Japanese public broadcaster NHK has triggered controversy among Japanese viewers, with some critics saying the program downplayed the issue of the enshrinement of Class-A war criminals. Despite side-stepping deep discussions of the shrine's postwar role, the documentary still triggered a backlash from some right-wing groups in Japan, exposing the deep-rooted misconceptions and increasingly radical nature of Japan's right-wing forces, a Chinese expert said. The special program "Yasukuni Shrine: Secret Records — The Blank Postwar History" was aired on Sunday. Before the broadcast, NHK published a preview saying "secret records" were disclosed for the first time in the documentary, containing details of the previously unknown "blank pages of history", including the behind-the-scenes process surrounding the enshrinement of Class-A war criminals. Through analyzing internal documents and interviews with over 200 people connected to the issue, the program revealed the decision-making process including the agreement on enshrinement in 1969, later changes to the decision, and the enshrinement of the notorious Class-A war criminals in 1978. Some Japanese observers said these documents show there was no immediate unanimous approval within Yasukuni Shrine for the enshrinement of Class-A war criminals. The way war criminals were handled is closely linked to the issue of Japan's war responsibility, making the release of these materials highly significant. Others commented that the program serves as powerful education for the general public, and the internal audio recordings and video footage are particularly rare. Since the enshrinement, Japanese politicians have continuously visited the Yasukuni Shrine or placed offerings there, provoking strong discontent among Asian countries including China and South Korea which were invaded by Japan during WWII. Following the broadcast, the documentary drew heated discussions online. Some viewers criticized the program for treating the enshrinement of Class-A war criminals too lightly and failing to sufficiently discuss the Yasukuni Shrine's role beyond mourning the war dead. A netizen @keishi_001 criticized the program for changing the shrine's rhetoric of "consolation of souls" and "honoring" to "how to mourn" and muddling the distinction between them. Such wording "doesn't at all highlight the danger of Yasukuni Shrine's role as a facility that glorifies the war dead, praises their virtues and passes them down", and the documentary didn't depict why China and South Korea react with opposition, or "the role of the shrine as the ideological pillar for war mobilization in the regions it invaded or colonized." However, even this understatement in the program triggered opposing criticism from some viewers, including one X user who claimed "there is no duty to abandon the spirit of honoring the war dead and their families", adding that NHK is "desperate to smear Japan at any cost." Zhou Yongsheng, a professor at China Foreign Affairs University, told the Global Times that the reactions surrounding the documentary reflected the extent to which some Japanese right-wing forces have moved in a direction of historical distortion. Some people in Japan have portrayed war criminals as "heroes", Zhou said, citing a narrative advocated by people including former Japanese prime ministers Shinzo Abe and Junichiro Koizumi that the sacrifices of those who died in the war helped lay the foundation for peace. This type of narrative completely distorts history. The invasion, which Japan initiated and has failed to sincerely reflect on to this day, did not lay the foundation for peace or Japan's development, but rather undermined Japan's capability of healthy and peaceful development and its postwar credibility among its neighbors, Zhou said. Since the enshrinement of the Class-A war criminals, Japanese politicians have either visited or provided ritual offerings, which triggered strong backlashes from victim countries including China and South Korea. This year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial. On August 15, although Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has not personally set foot in the Yasukuni Shrine, she offered ritual fees in her capacity as president of the Liberal Democratic Party. Some cabinet members, including Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, visited the shrine in person. Such moves have once again put the Yasukuni issue into the spotlight. Amid this trend, Atsushi Koketsu, a professor emeritus at Yamaguchi University in Japan, told the Global Times that politicians had held back from visiting Yasukuni for a certain period of time. But since the Takaichi administration took office, Japan's drift toward militarism has become unmistakable. The Japanese people should recognize that such behavior is wrong. "I personally define Yasukuni Shrine as a 'shrine of aggression'. Therefore, I believe that such visits carry the danger of reenacting the past wars of aggression," Atsushi said. Responding to these visits, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson said earlier in August that during WWII, Japan launched the war of aggression and committed horrendous crimes. The Yasukuni war shrine is a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism. It is in fact a shrine for war criminals, as it honors 14 convicted Class-A war criminals responsible for the war of aggression. "No pretext whatsoever can hide the Japanese politicians' true intention, which is to change the verdict on the war criminals, cover up Japan's war crimes, distort historical facts, and pave the way for accelerating remilitarization. This is an affront to historical justice, a challenge to the foundational norms of civilization, and a provocation against the postwar international order. Such behavior has been firmly rejected by the overwhelming majority of the international community," the spokesperson said. China urged Japan to seriously reflect on its history of aggression, make a clean break with militarism, and regain the trust of Asian neighbors and the international community through concrete actions, said the spokesperson.

item.title: Historical trend of China-Latin America cooperation moving toward mutual engagement will not change: official
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 21:05:00
A symposium on China-Latin America relations is held on October 12, 2026 in Beijing, where Chinese officials and experts share views about the development of China-Latin America relations. Photo: Sun Langchen/GT Regardless of how the regional situation changes, the historical trend of China-Latin America cooperation moving toward mutual engagement will not change, Qiu Xiaoqi, special representative of the Chinese Government on Latin American Affairs, said on Monday. "China has consistently adhered to the principle of noninterference in internal affairs and respects the choices made by the people of Latin American countries," Qiu made the remarks during a symposium on China-Latin America relations held in Beijing, saying China firmly opposes the US blockade and sanctions against Cuba, and will continue to firmly support the Cuban people in pursuing a development path suited to their own national conditions, while opposing external interference and blockade. In response to a question on the rise of right-wing governments in some countries and closer ties between some regional countries and the US, Qiu told the Global Times that China does not draw ideological lines and is willing to develop friendly relations with all Latin American and Caribbean countries based on the one-China principle. The latest Latinobarómetro survey shows that regardless of whether left-wing or right-wing governments are in power, the proportion of Latin American people holding positive views of China's influence in the region has continued to rise. For individuals who stubbornly support separatist forces, China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its national sovereignty and territorial integrity, Qiu noted. Amid the rise of anti-globalization, the absence of rule of law in global affairs, growing governance deficits, and insufficient representation and voice of Global South countries in international affairs, Qiu highlighted the importance of a fairer global governance system amid rising geopolitical tensions, saying the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) is consistent with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter. "Global governance is not the privilege of a few countries, nor should power politics and rule monopoly be allowed," Qiu said, stressing that all countries, regardless of size or wealth, should enjoy equal rights to participate in international affairs and choose their own development paths. GGI has received support from nearly 160 countries and international organizations, while more than 60 countries have joined the Group of Friends of the Global Governance Initiative, Qiu said. For Latin America, development cooperation has become a key area of China's engagement with the region. Addressing the development deficit is "the most central and urgent task" of global governance, Qiu noted, adding that China and Latin American countries have expanded cooperation in infrastructure, energy, agriculture, green development and digital sectors. High-quality Belt and Road cooperation has continued to advance in Latin America and the Caribbean, with 24 countries in the region participating. China-Latin America trade reached $549 billion in 2025, a record high, while trade in the first eight months of this year totaled $422.64 billion, up 19.1 percent year-on-year. Experts said the cooperation is increasingly moving beyond traditional trade and infrastructure. Yue Yunxia, deputy director of the Institute of Latin American Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, cited projects including Peru's Chancay Port, Brazil's photovoltaic power projects and industrial parks in Trinidad and Tobago as examples of China-Latin America cooperation expanding into new infrastructure, digital transformation and technological innovation. "China and Latin America are steadily moving from trade partners toward a development community," Yue said. Concrete cooperation has also improved livelihoods. China has implemented 119 "small yet impactful" livelihood projects in Latin America, covering medical services, housing and renewable energy. The "Silk Road Ark" hospital ship has provided humanitarian medical services in several Latin American countries, while Chinese assistance in areas such as photovoltaic equipment and social housing has benefited local communities. Chen Dong, a specially appointed research fellow at the Research Center on Building a Community with a Shared Future for Humanity, cited the introduction of China's Juncao technology to other countries to help farmers increase incomes and improve food security, as well as police training cooperation to strengthen security capabilities. "One stalk of grass can bring hope," Chen said, referring to the Juncao technology promoted in more than 110 countries and regions. "GGI needs concrete actions to ensure that achievements benefit people in all countries." Looking ahead, Chinese officials said cooperation in emerging areas such as AI could become a new frontier for global governance. The cooperation on global AI governance should focus on three areas: ensuring fair access to AI capabilities, promoting coordination on rules and accountability, and increasing the participation and representation of Global South countries in AI governance, Yue said. China advocates open and win-win cooperation to drive innovative development, comprehensively promote AI technological innovation, industrial development and application scenarios, enhance risk awareness, ensure security and controllability, and ensure that AI remains under human control. "AI should become a powerful positive force for improving people's well-being and advancing human civilization," Yue said.

item.title: China urges Japan's leaders to heed voices of justice at home: FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 18:33:00
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning In response to former Japanese foreign minister and Chair of the Association for the Promotion of International Trade Takeshi Iwaya's remarks following his visit to China that Japan was responsible for the deterioration in China-Japan relations and that the Japanese government should seek ways to improve ties, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said the remarks reflected the rationality and conscience of insightful people in Japan and were positively viewed by China. When asked to comment on the voices in Japan that criticize the evasion of historical responsibility for leading Japan’s China policy astray and call on the Japanese government to face up to and address the problem, Mao said during a press briefing on Monday that as they pointed out, the root cause and essence of the problem lie in the serious distortions and errors in the Japanese leadership’s view of history and of China, which have severely undermined the political foundation of China-Japan relations. Mao said that this situation serves the interests of neither side, and Japan bears full responsibility for it, adding that the onus was on Japan to put bilateral ties back on track. We urge Japan’s current leaders to listen to and heed voices of justice at home, face up to the root causes of the problems, abide by the four political documents between China and Japan, and genuinely reflect on and correct their mistakes on issues concerning Taiwan island, history and their understanding of China, Mao added. Global Times
